title: There's an Active Volcano Under Antarctica — And It Rains Gold
youtube_description:
Antarctica isn't just ice. It's an iceberg of secrets, and they get stranger the deeper you go.

At the surface: the world's largest iceberg, A23a, calved off the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in 1986 — then sat grounded on the seafloor for over thirty years before it finally broke free and started drifting in 2020. Four kilometres down is Lake Vostok, a subglacial lake roughly the size of Lake Ontario that's been sealed off from sunlight for an estimated fifteen million years. Scientists have since pulled ice cores from the continent over 1.2 million years old — a direct, frozen record of Earth's atmosphere from before humans existed.

Then it gets stranger. Under Taylor Glacier, a pocket of ancient seawater called Blood Falls has stayed sealed for roughly 1.5 million years, still liquid, still red from oxidized iron, and still hosting microbial life that has never once seen sunlight. And at the bottom of it all sits Mount Erebus, the world's southernmost active volcano — one of only eight places on Earth with a permanent lava lake, continuously active since at least 1972. It also vents an estimated 80 grams of microscopic gold dust into the air every single day.
